lesson.title: Capstone: Build a Software-Defined Network Testbed
lesson.summary: This capstone has you build a small software-defined network using Linux network namespaces to simulate multiple hosts and switches, connected through an OpenFlow-capable switch and controlled by an SDN controller program you write yourself.
lesson.body:
This project builds a working, if miniature, software-defined network entirely on a single machine, so you can see, run, and break the control plane and data plane separation that defines SDN, without needing a rack of physical switches. The three pieces you assemble are a simulated topology, an OpenFlow-capable switch, and a controller you program.

Network namespaces, covered earlier in the course, are what make the simulated topology possible. Each namespace gives you an isolated network stack, its own interfaces, routing table, and so on, all running on top of one Linux kernel, so a handful of namespaces can stand in for a handful of separate hosts. Connect them with virtual Ethernet links, and you have a small topology, say four hosts and one switch, without touching any real hardware. In place of a traditional switch, run an OpenFlow-capable virtual switch such as Open vSwitch. Unlike a traditional switch, which decides how to forward each packet using logic built into its own firmware, an OpenFlow switch forwards packets according to a flow table that an external controller installs into it, using the OpenFlow protocol to say things like, match packets that look like this, then do that: forward out this port, drop it, or send it up to the controller for a decision.

The interesting part of this capstone is the SDN controller you write yourself, which is where the control plane and data plane separation stops being an abstract diagram and becomes something you can watch happen. A good starting point is making the controller behave like an ordinary learning switch: when a packet arrives whose source address the controller has not seen before, it learns which port that host is on, and forwards the packet based on what it already knows about the destination, exactly replicating standard Ethernet switching behavior, just with the decision made by your controller code instead of switch firmware. Once that baseline works, extend the controller with logic that a traditional switch could never do on its own: routing different flows across two different paths based on current utilization, blocking traffic between two specific hosts as a simple firewall policy, or detecting a link failure and rerouting affected flows around it.

Concretely, imagine writing a controller that, when it sees the very first packet of a new connection, checks which of two available paths through your topology currently has more capacity available, picks one, and installs a flow table entry in the relevant switches so that every subsequent packet in that same connection takes the chosen path automatically, without needing to ask the controller again. This is the actual motivation behind SDN in real networks: because one piece of software has a global view of the whole topology, it can make forwarding decisions that would be difficult or impossible for switches making decisions independently, each with visibility into only its own local traffic.

Because the entire testbed lives in namespaces on one machine, you can tear it down and rebuild it in seconds, which makes it a genuinely useful place to experiment. Deliberately kill a virtual link to see whether your controller notices and reroutes around it. Watch, in real time, exactly which packets get sent up to the controller for a decision versus which ones a switch forwards on its own using an already installed flow rule. By the time your controller can handle a link failure gracefully, you will have built, from the ground up, both a switch and the centralized brain that controls it, and you will be able to point to exactly which decisions moved from being made independently at each device to being made once, centrally, and pushed out to the hardware, which is the entire idea SDN is built on.
